question: What is the difference between RPO (Recovery Point Objective) and RTO (Recovery Time Objective)? What is the difference between RPO (Recovery Point Objective) and RTO (Recovery Time Objective)?

options.text: RPO: maximum acceptable data loss measured in time; RTO: maximum acceptable downtime until service restoration.
RPO: maximum acceptable downtime until service restoration; RTO: maximum acceptable data loss measured in time, the reverse of the standard definitions.
RPO and RTO both measure the same thing, downtime, but RPO is expressed in minutes while RTO is expressed as a percentage of uptime (e.g. 99.9%).
RPO: the total dollar cost of a data loss incident; RTO: the total dollar cost of downtime, both derived financially rather than measured in time.

explanation: Specification answer: RPO: maximum acceptable data loss measured in time; RTO: maximum acceptable downtime until service restoration.

question: Explain Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR) in relational databases.? Explain Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR) in relational databases.

options.text: Restoring a base physical backup and replaying continuous Write-Ahead Logs (WAL/binlog) up to an exact specific microsecond timestamp.
Restoring only the most recent full backup and discarding all WAL/binlog segments, since a full backup by itself already represents the most recent consistent point in time.
Replaying WAL/binlog segments alone, without ever restoring a base backup first, since the log is assumed to contain the complete history of every row from table creation.
Taking a new backup at the exact moment recovery is needed, rather than restoring an older backup at all, so PITR only works if the failure is anticipated in advance.

explanation: Specification answer: Restoring a base physical backup and replaying continuous Write-Ahead Logs (WAL/binlog) up to an exact specific microsecond timestamp.

question: What is the Expand/Contract (Parallel Run) pattern in database migrations? What is the Expand/Contract (Parallel Run) pattern in database migrations?

options.text: Expand: add new column/table while maintaining old; Contract: migrate application traffic to new structure, then drop old structure online.
Expand: drop the old column/table immediately to force all writers onto the new structure; Contract: add the new structure only after traffic has already fully migrated.
Expand and Contract both happen in a single offline maintenance window, since online schema changes are not possible with this pattern.
Expand: migrate application traffic to the new structure immediately; Contract: add the new column/table afterward once traffic has already moved, keeping both live indefinitely.

explanation: Specification answer: Expand: add new column/table while maintaining old; Contract: migrate application traffic to new structure, then drop old structure online.

question: Why should zero-downtime migrations set strict statementtimeout and locktimeout? Why should zero-downtime migrations set strict statementtimeout and locktimeout?

options.text: To abort immediately if an exclusive lock cannot be acquired within milliseconds, preventing blocking application traffic queues.
To make the migration run faster by skipping the transaction log entirely when statement_timeout is set, trading durability for speed.
To ensure the migration retries indefinitely in a tight loop until it succeeds, since a timeout error is treated as a signal to retry immediately rather than to abort.
To guarantee the migration acquires its lock before any other query, by making every other transaction's lock requests wait behind the migration's queued request.

explanation: Specification answer: To abort immediately if an exclusive lock cannot be acquired within milliseconds, preventing blocking application traffic queues.

question:
During triage in Production DBRE Backups Migrations HA, an engineer observes:
"System fault during operation: Exclusive Table Lock Starvation During Online Schema Migration".
What is the verified root cause?

options.text: Migration script runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN statuscode INT; without a locktimeout, blocking behind a slow query and queuing all incoming web requests.

The ALTER TABLE statement itself completes instantly since adding a nullable column is metadata-only, but a separate backfill UPDATE statement run immediately after holds the row lock that blocks the queue.

lock_timeout was set correctly, but statement_timeout was left at its default of zero (no timeout), so the ALTER TABLE itself runs indefinitely once it does acquire the lock, still queuing traffic behind it.

The migration correctly uses a short lock_timeout and retries on failure, but each retry re-queues at the back of the same lock wait queue behind the same slow query, so the effective wait time is unbounded even though each individual attempt is short.

explanation:
Root Cause: Migration script runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN statuscode INT; without a locktimeout, blocking behind a slow query and queuing all incoming web requests.

Fix Resolution:
Set strict lock timeout before running DDL: SET locktimeout = '2s'; ALTER TABLE ....
